readerTitle: The ramen shop that raised money and lost its line
caseNote: 가상 사례 (라멘 가게, 물류 회사 사내 팀) + 실제 기업 (Mailchimp, softwareNote에서만 언급) · 라멘 가게와 사내 팀의 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 투자는 성공의 보상이 아니라 미래(지분, 속도, 기대치)를 현금과 바꾸는 거래이며, 돈이 진짜 병목일 때만 남는 거래다.
misconception: 투자를 받을 수 있으면 받는 게 좋다. 돈이 많을수록 사업은 더 빨리, 더 안전하게 큰다.

sources.text: 라멘 가게와 물류 회사 사내 팀 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시
Intuit press release (September 2021): Intuit to acquire Mailchimp for approximately $12 billion

factChecks.note: 가상 계산 확인: 투자 $1.5M에 지분 30% → 투자 후 기업가치 $5M. 투자자가 5배 회수를 기대하면 $1.5M × 5 = $7.5M, 30% 지분이 $7.5M이 되려면 회사 전체 가치 $7.5M ÷ 0.3 = $25M.
Mailchimp: 2001년 창업, 외부 벤처 투자 없이 성장, 2021년 Intuit가 약 120억 달러에 인수 발표. 게시 전 Intuit 보도자료로 금액과 '외부 투자 없음' 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
사내 팀 사례($2M, 15명, 12개 지역, 연료비 10% 절감 목표)는 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The ramen shop that raised money and lost its line
body: Mika's ramen shop has a queue every night and a steady profit. Investors offer $1.5 million to open five more shops in two years.
Three years later, four of the new shops have closed. The original is still busy. But Mika now owns 70% of it, and owes her investors a story about growth that never came.

image.label: A busy ramen shop next to empty shuttered branches
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 왼쪽에 손님 줄이 길게 늘어선 작은 라멘 가게, 오른쪽에 셔터가 내려진 같은 간판의 가게 네 곳. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Take the $1.5 million?
body: You're Mika, before the deal. One shop earns about $150,000 a year in profit. Your chef is the reason people queue.
Investors offer $1.5 million for 30% of the company. They want five new shops within two years. What do you do?

options.text: Take it. Lines like yours don't last, so grow while demand is hot
options.feedback: You get speed and a safety cushion. You also take on a promise to grow five times over, with one chef and no proof a second shop works.

options.text: Decline for now. Open a second shop from profits, then decide
options.feedback: You grow slower and carry more personal risk. In return you learn whether the shop can be copied before you sell part of it.

options.text: Take it, but negotiate down to three new shops
options.feedback: Fewer shops lowers the strain. But the money still expects big growth, and you still haven't tested whether shop two works.

cards.title: What the money came with.
body: The cash was the easy part. The expectation attached to it was the hard part.

breakdown.label: Cash in
breakdown.detail: For new shops, staff and fit-out

breakdown.label: Ownership given
breakdown.detail: Of every future profit and sale

breakdown.label: Hoped-for return
breakdown.detail: If investors want 5 times their money

cards.callout: A shop earning $150,000 a year had to become a $25 million company.

cards.title: Outside money is a trade, not a prize.
body: **Raising money** means swapping part of your future, such as ownership, control and pace, for cash now.
That trade pays off only when cash is what holds you back, and the business can grow into what the money expects back.
Mika's limit was never cash. It was one chef, one recipe and one proven location. Money let her copy the shop before she knew it could be copied.

image.label: A scale: cash on one side, ownership and expectations on the other
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 한쪽에 "Cash now" 돈주머니, 다른 쪽에 "Ownership", "Control", "Growth expected" 블록 세 개. 저울이 기대치 쪽으로 살짝 기울어 있음.

cards.title: Three questions before you raise.
body: Before taking anyone's money, answer these plainly.
list: **What will the money buy?** Name it: a machine, a hire, a second location.
**Is cash the bottleneck?** Or is it people, demand or know-how that money can't speed up?
**Can the business reach the size the money expects?** Investors who own a share need that share to grow a lot.
cards.callout: If an answer is unclear, money mostly helps you make the mistake faster.
cards.softwareNote: Mailchimp grew for about two decades without venture investors and was bought by Intuit in 2021 for about $12 billion. Software can raise cheaply, but it can also often grow from customer revenue alone.

cards.title: You raise money inside companies too.
body: A manager asking leadership for a bigger budget is making the same trade. The extra money arrives with bigger targets, closer attention and less room to change course.
A small budget lets a team learn quietly. A large one turns a guess into a public promise. The question is the same as Mika's: is money really what's slowing you down?

cards.title: Not raising has costs too.
body: Growing from profits is slower. You may carry personal risk, and a funded rival can grab locations, staff or customers first.
In some markets, speed decides the winner, such as products that get more useful as more people join. There, waiting can cost more than selling a share.
The goal isn't to avoid outside money. It's to take it only for something you already know works.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a logistics company.
body: Your small team built a route tool that saves drivers time in one region. Leadership offers $2 million and 15 people to roll it out to all 12 regions this year, with a target of 10% fuel savings company-wide.

options.text: Accept the full budget. This much support may not come again
options.feedback: You get resources and visibility. But you haven't shown the savings hold outside one region, and a missed company-wide target can end the project.

options.text: Ask for a smaller budget to prove it in two more regions, then scale
options.feedback: You give up some speed and risk losing momentum. You gain proof that the tool works elsewhere before you promise 12 regions.

options.text: Decline extra money and grow slowly on your current budget
options.feedback: You keep control and avoid big targets. But if the tool truly works, moving this slowly may cost the company savings and your sponsor's interest.

cards.title: Raise money for what's proven, not for what's hoped.
body: Outside money buys speed and charges you in ownership and expectations. Take it when cash is the real limit and the business can grow into the promise.
**Try it today:** write down the one thing that most limits your growth right now. Then ask honestly whether more money would fix it.
